# Does bottom-up molten-salt TES economics hold up at 5 MWh vs. lithium-ion?

**Short answer: No.** At 5 MWh, molten-salt thermal energy storage (TES) costs roughly **4–5× more per MWh delivered** than a comparably-sized lithium-ion battery, because two *scale* penalties — a fixed-cost-dominated tank/BOP floor and a collapsed small-turbine efficiency — swamp the fact that the storage medium (salt) is intrinsically cheap. Molten-salt TES only becomes competitive at utility/GWh scale, paired with a free heat source (concentrated sunlight or waste heat) rather than purchased grid electricity, or in very long-duration/very-high-cycle-count applications.

## 1. Bottom-up installed cost: 5 MWh_t (thermal storage capacity), storage-only basis

**Basis:** "5 MWh" is read as 5,000 kWh of **thermal** storage capacity (nameplate). This section costs the storage hardware only (tanks, salt, pumps/HX/piping/controls, contingency/EPC) — the power block and electric heaters needed to actually charge/discharge it as an *electric battery* are added separately in Section 2, so the basis is explicit and the two don't get double-counted.

**Physical build-up:**
- Operating window: 290 °C (cold) → 565 °C (hot), ΔT = 275 K — standard solar-salt practice (melting range ≈222–238 °C measured by DSC in Fuentes et al. 2019; thermal-stability ceiling ≈585–600 °C from CSP literature)
- Specific heat of 60/40 NaNO₃/KNO₃ "solar salt": **1.52–1.61 kJ/kg·K** (measured, Fuentes et al. 2019)
- Salt mass = 5,000 kWh × 3,600 / (1.56 kJ/kg·K × 275 K) ≈ **42 t** nominal, +15% dead-salt/ullage margin → **~48 t** purchased
- Density ≈1,730–1,910 kg/m³ (literature estimate, not independently verified this session) → tanks sized at **~29 m³ (cold)** and **~32 m³ (hot)**

| Component | Basis / unit cost | Central cost | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Salt media (~48 t) | Small-lot nitrate-salt price ~$1,000/t (historical range $1,000–10,000/t per industry reporting; small purchase ≠ utility bulk discount) | **$48,300** | $24,150–$96,600 |
| Tanks (hot: stainless ~$12/kg bare shell; cold: carbon steel ~$4/kg; ×3 installed multiplier for insulation, heat-trace, nozzles, foundation) | ~4.1–4.4 t steel shell each, sized from salt volume | **$209,000** | $105,000–$315,000 |
| Balance of plant (hot/cold salt pumps, salt-to-steam HX, interconnect piping/insulation, I&C, sized for ~1 MWt/5h duty) | No vendor quote obtained — synthesized from small-industrial-skid cost practice | **$740,000** | $440,000–$1,050,000 |
| **Direct cost subtotal** | | **≈$1.00M** | $0.57M–$1.46M |
| Contingency (7–15%, central 10%) | Anchored to NREL/SAM CSP cost-model figures (7–9.5%), widened for small/first-of-kind risk | +$100,000 | +$40,000–$220,000 |
| Indirect/EPC/owner costs (20–35%, central 28%) | Anchored to NREL/SAM's 25.8% CSP-plant indirect-cost figure, transferred to a standalone skid | +$307,000 | +$122,000–$588,000 |
| **Total installed cost** | | **≈$1.40M** | **$0.73M–$2.27M** |
| **Installed cost per kWh_t** | ÷ 5,000 kWh_t | **≈$281/kWh_t** | **$146–$454/kWh_t** |

**Scale cross-check:** NREL/Sandia's molten-salt power-tower cost model (Turchi & Heath, NREL/TP-5500-57625, 2013) puts installed TES direct cost at **$27–$35.5/kWh_t** for a reference 115 MWe/10-hour utility CSP plant (~2,500–2,740 MWh_t, ~500× larger than this system). That's roughly **9× cheaper per kWh_t** than the 5 MWh build above — an implied cost-vs-capacity scaling exponent of about −0.35, consistent with the classic industrial "six-tenths rule." **The salt itself is cheap (~$48K of $1.4M); it's the fixed tank/pump/HX/controls floor that doesn't shrink with size that kills small-scale economics.**

## 2. Levelized cost of delivered electricity (amortized over cycle life)

To compare against a battery (electricity-in/electricity-out), the storage-only system above needs charging and discharging equipment added, and the round-trip efficiency penalty of doing that at small scale has to be priced in.

**Added hardware:**
- Charging: resistive electric heaters, ~98% efficient, ~$100/kW → **+$100,000** (range $50K–150K)
- Discharging: a small (~250 kWe) steam/ORC power block. Carnot ceiling at 565 °C/25 °C ≈ **64.4%**; utility-scale steam cycles capture ~65% of that ceiling (≈42% actual, per NREL/SAM). A ~250 kWe unit is assumed to capture only ~31–44% of the ceiling (**20–28% actual, central 25%**) — turbine/generator/parasitic losses scale badly at small size. Installed cost at this tiny rating, where no standard commercial product was identified, is assumed at **$3,000–6,000/kW** (central $4,500/kW) → **+$1,125,000** (range $750K–$1,500K)

**Total Scenario-A capex:** ≈**$2.63M** central (range $1.53M–$3.92M)

**Round-trip efficiency (electricity-in → electricity-out):** 0.98 (charge) × 0.90–0.97 (thermal retention, small tanks lose more than utility tanks) × 0.20–0.28 (power block) ≈ **18–27%, central ~23%** — far below a typical battery.

**Amortization assumptions:** 300 cycles/year (1/day, allowing downtime), **30-year design life** (per NREL's cited TES tank/hardware life), 7% real discount rate (CRF ≈8.06%), 2% O&M.

- Annual electricity delivered: 300 cycles × 5,000 kWh_t × 0.93 (retention) × 0.25 (power block) ≈ **349 MWh/yr** (range 225–475 MWh/yr)
- Annual cost: capex×CRF + O&M ≈ **$264,000/yr** (range $146K–$414K)
- **Levelized cost: ≈$758/MWh delivered, range $308–$1,840/MWh**

*(Context only, not the headline comparison: if the same hardware delivers **heat** rather than re-electrified power — e.g., for industrial process heat — there's no power-block penalty, and the levelized cost drops to roughly **$108/MWh_t of heat delivered**. That's a fundamentally different, more favorable comparison and isn't a substitute for the battery-vs-battery verdict below.)*

## 3. Lithium-ion at comparable scale, and the verdict

**Li-ion assumptions (5 MWh / ~1.25 MW, 4-hour class):**
- Installed cost: **$200–400/kWh** (central $300/kWh) for US utility-scale systems in 2024–25 — this session could not directly verify NREL ATB's current figure (network access to nrel.gov failed), so this is carried as a general-knowledge estimate, not a primary read. (A directly-verified global benchmark, outside the US/China, put long-duration BESS at **$125/kWh** as of Oct. 2025 — Ember/Mercom India — underscoring that US costs sit well above the global floor.)
- Cycle life: 4,000–6,000 cycles to 80% DoD; calendar life 12–20 years (central 15 yr); AC-AC round-trip efficiency 85–92%
- Same 300 cycles/yr, 7% discount rate, 1.5–2.5% O&M, applied symmetrically for a fair comparison

| | Capex | Annual cost | Annual delivered | **Levelized cost** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **5 MWh molten-salt TES (electric battery)** | $2.63M central | ~$264K/yr | ~349 MWh/yr | **~$758/MWh** (range $308–$1,840) |
| **5 MWh lithium-ion BESS** | $1.5M central | ~$195K/yr | ~1,200 MWh/yr (80% DoD) | **~$162/MWh** (range $78–$302) |

**Verdict: Lithium-ion wins decisively at this scale — roughly 4.7× cheaper per MWh delivered at central estimates.** The ranges barely overlap: only TES's most favorable case ($308/MWh) and Li-ion's least favorable case ($302/MWh) come close; across the bulk of the plausible range there's no contest.

**When does each technology actually win?**
- **Lithium-ion wins** whenever the application is short-duration (hours), grid-electricity-charged, and at anything from kWh up through tens-of-MWh scale — i.e., essentially all of today's commercial battery-storage market. It also improves further as Li-ion costs keep falling with manufacturing scale, while small TES costs are fixed-cost-bound with no comparable learning curve.
- **Molten-salt TES wins** only when (a) **deployment scale is utility/GWh-class** (removing the fixed-cost penalty — cost per kWh_t drops ~9× between 5 MWh and ~2,700 MWh_t), (b) **the heat input is free or low-cost** (concentrated sunlight in a CSP plant, or industrial waste heat) rather than purchased grid electricity — this is how virtually every real molten-salt TES installation is actually built, sidestepping the round-trip-efficiency problem entirely, and (c) duration and cumulative cycle count are very high, since TES tanks have an effectively unlimited cycle life (30-year calendar life, no capacity degradation) versus Li-ion's finite cycle life — an advantage that only matters once cycling is frequent/extreme enough for Li-ion replacement costs to bite.

**Key caveat (surfaced via inversion/pre-mortem check on the premise itself):** every molten-salt TES cost source found in this research — the NREL/SAM cost model, the broader CSP literature — describes either utility/GWh-scale plants paired with concentrating solar collection, or industrial process-heat systems. **No standalone, grid-charged, MWh-class molten-salt "battery" product appears to exist in the market.** This 5 MWh comparison is therefore a synthetic, from-first-principles construction, not a benchmarked product price — which is exactly *why* a bottom-up build was necessary rather than quoting an industry number, but it also means the result should be read as explaining *why the industry doesn't build systems this way* rather than as a quote a developer could act on. The dominant sources of uncertainty in the numbers above are the un-vendor-quoted tank/BOP/small-power-block costs (each could plausibly be off 2× in either direction) and the unverified Li-ion cost benchmark — so treat the point estimates as illustrative, but the *direction* of the verdict (Li-ion wins at this scale) as robust.
